correctness.rationale: Trace identities give constant squared norm 1/3. For any two trace-zero ternary forms, an orthonormal A-null basis and connectedness of the indefinite projective conic give a simultaneous isotropic vector. Hence both squared distances from any two prescribed centers at that point are 1/3 plus the respective center norms squared, proving the quantified two-center obstruction and optimizer rigidity. Three unoriented planar axes 60 degrees apart ensure a minimum squared projection at most 1/4 with equality; three negative projector centers at coefficient 1/8 consequently give exactly squared covering radius 21/64. The center matrices correspond to positive definite trace-one states (eigenvalues 1/4,3/8,3/8). All quantifiers, boundary cases and normalization are explicit; finite computational checks are corroborative only.

originality.rationale: The new claim is a complete sharp critical-count theorem for when the Veronese surface covering radius first decreases, including every optimal two-center arrangement and an explicit radius-certified three-center configuration. The underlying simultaneous-null-form fact and the two-center implication are directly related to Brickman’s classical joint-numerical-range convexity and are NOT novel standalone assertions. The motivating 2026 paper studies the six-ball noncovering barrier at radius 1/2, a different regime and objective. Targeted historical and semantic comparisons found no statement implying this combined threshold; unindexed projective quantization literature remains a priority risk.
residual_risks: The two-center simultaneous quadratic zero lemma and its covering implication follow from classical Brickman convexity; novelty is confined to the sharp combined count with explicit strict three-center witness.
An unindexed older quantization or k-center analysis of the Veronese projective plane may imply the same critical-count result.
The optimal radius for three balls is not known here; the stated sqrt(21)/8 is the exact covering radius of the exhibited centers, not the global optimum.

Brickman original primary article and the 2005 full text were not inspected; their broad theorem descriptions are sufficient to acknowledge classical coverage but not to exclude all derived consequences.

value.rationale: The diameter-one five-dimensional Veronese surface is a current natural object in Grünbaum equal-diameter covering geometry. Its minimal number of balls needed merely to beat the circumradius is a geometrically intrinsic threshold. The exact count three is sharp, with complete two-center optimizer rigidity and a simple explicit inside-the-convex-hull three-center witness. This does not resolve the six-ball radius-1/2 obstruction or the exact global three-center radius; those limits are explicit. The result is a motivated nontrivial covering-geometry property of the new object, not a free parameter restatement.
